---
name: commit-work
description: Stage and commit Git changes so each commit holds only the approved change, leaving content the user already staged untouched, splitting mixed hunks without an interactive terminal, verifying the staged version rather than the working tree, and writing Conventional Commits messages. Use when asked to commit, check in or save work to git, stage selected files or hunks, split a mixed tree into commits, review what is staged, or draft a commit message. Not for rebasing, squashing, amending or force-pushing history, resolving merge conflicts, opening pull requests, or code review unrelated to a commit.
---

# Commit work

Split commits by behavior, not by file type: an implementation and the tests that pin it go in the same commit.

## Route by intent first

| The user asks to | Run | Never |
|---|---|---|
| draft a message | use the diff the user supplied as is; with none, read-only inspection only (`git status`, `git diff --cached`, `git log`); reply with the message text only | run or propose a command that changes the index or creates a commit, `git commit -F` included |
| review what is staged | steps 1 and 4, report findings | change the index or the tree |
| stage changes | steps 1-4 in the real index, stop after the review | run or propose `git commit`, or change entries the user already staged |
| commit | steps 1-8 | commit anything outside the approved set |

When the user asks for proposed commands, label them as proposed and do not claim they ran.

## Workflow

1. Read `git status`, `git diff --cached` and `git diff`. Stop and ask when `git status` reports a merge, rebase, cherry-pick or revert in progress (see Gotchas), when conflicts remain, or when there is nothing to commit (never an empty or invented commit). Anything staged before you started is the user's. Never include it in a commit without the user's approval; when only other paths are approved and it must stay out, use the temporary index in step 3.
2. Plan each commit as paths, plus hunks for a mixed file. Split a feature from a refactor, formatting from logic, and a dependency bump from a behavior change. Never split by layer (backend vs frontend) or tests from the code they pin; the rule at the top wins.
3. Stage. Scratch files (temporary index, patches, message, verify export) go in a run directory of their own, so concurrent or leftover runs never collide. Do the leftover check and the `mktemp -d` below for the first commit of the run only; a later commit of the same run reuses its `<run>` (step 8). First list `<gitdir>/commit-work.*` (`git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`): report any you find and never delete them, since another run may own them. Then create yours with `mktemp -d "$(git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir)/commit-work.XXXXXX"` and write the printed path, `<run>` below, literally into every later command. Every route that ends the run (stage-only done, a stop, a failed check in step 5 or 7, or the last commit) removes it with `rm -rf -- "<run>"` before replying, or names it as left behind and why. Two questions pick the index, then the method:
   - Which index? Commit request and the user has staged content that must stay out: a temporary index, so the real one stays as the user left it. Every other case, stage-only requests included: the real index; leave the user's entries in it alone. When the user approved a path's staged diff, commit that exact staged version and never restage the whole working-tree file over it: leave it in the real index, or copy it into the temporary index with `git diff --cached --binary -- <path> > <run>/staged.diff` and `GIT_INDEX_FILE=<run>/index git apply --cached <run>/staged.diff`. That capture always reads the real index, so run it before any command sets `GIT_INDEX_FILE` or writes `<run>/staged.diff`; the order is capture, then build the temporary index, then apply. Ask only when it is unclear whether the staged diff is approved or which hunks are intended.
     Overlap check, real index, before staging anything: `git diff --cached --name-only -- <approved paths>` lists approved paths that already hold staged content. Any listed path whose staged diff the user did not approve: stop and ask, and never run the step 8 `git reset` on it, because that unstages the user's hunk. A listed path whose staged diff the user did approve: commit that exact staged version, do not restage the working-tree file over it, and continue. When an approved path also has unstaged edits, `git add -- <path>` would replace the approved staged blob: never `git add` that path; leave its staged version in the real index, or copy it into the temporary index with `git diff --cached --binary -- <path>` and `git apply --cached`.
     Stage-only, before staging anything: record `git ls-files -s -- <the user's staged paths>` (step 4 compares against this record).
     For the temporary index, first capture the approved staged patches above from the real index (no prefix; the one exemption to the prefix rule), then note `git rev-parse HEAD`, start with `GIT_INDEX_FILE=<run>/index git read-tree HEAD` (`read-tree --empty` instead when `git rev-parse --verify -q HEAD` prints nothing, as in a repository with no commits yet), and put that same `GIT_INDEX_FILE=` prefix on every git command of steps 3-7, including the re-inspection after a failed commit and `git show --stat`.
   - Whole file: `git add -- <paths>`. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`: they sweep in untracked artifacts. Never `git commit -a` or `-am` either: they stage every modified tracked file, the user's unapproved edits included.
   - Part of a tracked file (`git ls-files --error-unmatch -- <file>` succeeds): `git diff -U1 -- <file> > <run>/all.diff`, copy it to `<run>/pick.diff` without the unwanted hunks (delete whole hunks, keep the header), then `git apply --cached --check` and `git apply --cached` on the pick file. `pick.diff` keeps the `diff --git`, `index` and `---`/`+++` header lines and drops only whole `@@` hunks; if `git apply --cached --check` fails, stop and ask, and never edit inside a hunk. For an untracked file `git diff` prints nothing: ask whether the whole file is approved, or for its exact approved content, and never build a patch from `/dev/null`. `-U1` keeps nearby hunks apart; if the hunks you must separate still share one, ask instead of editing hunk counts. `git add -p` needs an interactive terminal. Read `references/split-one-file.md` when one file holds hunks for two different commits (a refactor and a bugfix, say).
4. Review the exact index. For a commit it holds only the approved change. For stage-only, review just the newly staged delta, and confirm the user's own entries are unchanged: `git ls-files -s -- <their paths>` after staging must match the record taken in step 3 before staging. Check for secrets, accidental debug logging, unrelated formatting churn, lockfile churn or generated output this change did not produce, a force-added ignored file (`git check-ignore --no-index -v <staged paths>` prints any), and a scope naming pre-move paths. Run `git diff --cached --check`: it warns about conflict markers and whitespace errors the change introduces; report any and ask before committing. Then describe the staged change in one or two sentences, what and why; if that is not clean, the commit is too big or mixed, so go back to step 2. For a review request (the route that runs steps 1 and 4 only), report instead that the staged set is mixed and name the split you would make; do not return to step 2 or change the index.
5. Verify the staged version with the fastest relevant check: tests for the touched paths, else lint, else build. Find the command in the repository itself: its test script for the touched paths (`package.json` scripts, Makefile targets, the CI config), else its lint script, else its build script; ask the user only when none exists. If `git diff --quiet` succeeds and no untracked file feeds the check, run it in place. Otherwise the tree is not the commit: export the index with `git checkout-index -a --prefix=<run>/verify/` (the trailing slash matters) and run the check there. The export holds tracked files only, so a check that needs installed dependencies (`node_modules`, a virtualenv, vendored packages) or untracked config cannot run there as is: link the project's dependency directories and the untracked config the check needs into `<run>/verify/` (for example `ln -s "$PWD/node_modules" <run>/verify/node_modules`), never copying secrets out of the repository, and run the check there. `<run>` sits inside the git directory, and some runners skip paths under `.git` (Jest's haste map, for example, then finds no tests): for those, export to a directory outside the repository instead: first `verify=$(mktemp -d) && echo "$verify"`, then `git checkout-index -a --prefix="<verify>/"`, with the printed path written literally (as step 3 requires for scratch paths) into that command and into the link, check and `rm -rf -- "<verify>"` commands; a stop names it as left behind like `<run>`. If it cannot run there even so (missing dependencies or untracked config), report "staged version not verified"; never pass off a worktree run as the commit's. On failure, stop, report and ask.
6. Take the message vocabulary from the repository, in the order of `references/commit-message-template.md`: commitlint config, `commit.template`, CONTRIBUTING, a PR template, then the type and scope vocabulary of recent subjects (`git log --format=%s -30`). Write Conventional Commits 1.0.0 when those sources use it; when two sources conflict, the reference's collect-and-ask step applies. Conventional Commits is the default only when all of those are absent (an empty or brand-new history). The body says why, and `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer marks only a real compatibility break. Commit with `-m` for one line, `-F <run>/msg.txt` for more; a bare `git commit` opens an editor an agent shell cannot drive. Add no trailers (`Co-Authored-By`, `Signed-off-by`, "Generated with") unless the user or the repository requires them. Read `references/commit-message-template.md` only when the repository sets its own message rules (commitlint config, commit template, CONTRIBUTING, PR template), you need footers beyond `BREAKING CHANGE`, or you want worked messages.
7. Just before `git commit`, in temporary-index mode confirm `git rev-parse HEAD` is still the commit you read the tree from; if another commit landed meanwhile, rebuild the index from the new HEAD, or your commit silently reverts it. Then run `git write-tree` and keep the tree ID. After a successful commit, compare it with `git rev-parse 'HEAD^{tree}'`. If they differ, a hook changed what was committed: show `git diff <tree> HEAD`, report it and ask. If the commit failed, do not retry it as is: run `git status` and `git diff --cached` again (hooks reformat and restage files), review, and treat a failed hook check as a step 5 failure (report and ask). Never propose `--no-verify`, not even as an option; use it only when the user asks for it by name, because it skips the checks the repository relies on. Never amend or add a fix-up commit without the user's say-so: amending rewrites a commit that may already be pushed or reviewed, and a fix-up splits one approved change across two commits.
8. Repeat steps 3-7 until the approved set is committed, not until the tree is clean. For each further commit, repeat only step 3's staging through step 7 in the same `<run>`: no new leftover check and no new `mktemp -d`, and in temporary-index mode rebuild the temporary index from the new HEAD as step 3 and `references/split-one-file.md` describe. Afterwards remove `<run>` (step 3) and, in temporary-index mode, run `git reset -q -- <committed paths>` so the real index stops showing them as a staged revert. Report each hash, subject and verification result, and list the staged and unstaged changes you left untouched. A commit request does not authorize `git push`: stop after the report and leave pushing to the user.

## Gotchas

- A commit joins whatever operation is in progress. During a merge it becomes the merge commit, with two parents and the other branch's changes. During a rebase it lands on a detached HEAD inside the rebased sequence and is lost if the rebase is aborted. During a cherry-pick or revert it concludes that operation; a cherry-pick commit keeps the picked commit's author.
- Agent harnesses usually start each tool call in a fresh shell, so an `export GIT_INDEX_FILE` or a `$run` variable does not carry over and the next command silently writes the real index. Write literal values into every command. For the same reason a cleanup `trap ... EXIT` fires when the call that set it ends; use one only when the whole run is a single shell call.
- `git commit -- <paths>` (`--only`) also leaves the rest of the index out, but it commits the whole working-tree file, unstaged hunks included. Use the temporary index.
- Never `git stash` to isolate or test: the stash stack is shared by every worktree of the repository, and another session can pop your entry or you theirs.
